## Introduction

In mid-20th century, the US Air Force faced a life threatening challenge. Planes got to be out of control for some pilots. Blames where on the men in the cockpits for the crashes, which lead to citing "pilot error" in crash reports as the main etiology. After a thorough investigation, it was found that the problem was not with the pilots but with the design of the cockpit itself. Back in early [@19^th], the engineers attempted, for first time ever to design a fighter plane cockpit that would fit the average pilot. By measuring hundreds of male pilots, all the size and shape of the seat and the helmet, the distance to the pedal and stick were designed to fit the average pilot, which served as a standard for more than two decades. However, in reality, out of 4063 pilots,no body fitted to the average based designed fighter plane cockpit. Not a single pilot actually matched those average dimensions across all parameters.[@rose_end_2016]

This historical encounter reflects similar challenge in the modern evidence-based medicine.[@kent_personalized_2018] In medical research, randomized controlled trial (RCT) is used to decide if a treatment is effective or not for a particular medical intervention. National and International guidelines for clinical service decision making developed based on this gold standard method for determining causal effects. [@kent_predictive_2020] However, the average treatment effect resulted that comes from RCT findings fail to answer the practicing clinician question regarding the most likely outcome of an intervention for a particular patient that appears to a clinical service setting. The primary reason for this is that real patient in clinical setting usually differs from the average patient in a trial[@willke_concepts_2012] [@kent_personalized_2018].

Modern trials increasingly enroll patients with less severe disease who are less likely to derive significant benefit from an intervention. Due to these, low risk patients derive minimal benefit, they influence the average effect size and reduce  statistical power of the trial, yielding negative or null results. As a result higher risk patients who actually possess the potential for a greater than observed benefit left under treatment and denied therapy. Conversely, trials tries not to enroll complex older patients with multiple commodities. Unfortunately, the findings from trials will be generalized to them in clinical practices. This in turn results in over treatment as these patients may suffer unique treatment related harms. [@greenfield_heterogeneity_2007] 

Trial results represent summary data from selected pool of patients, whereas individual response to treatment is will be explained by
a concept refereed as Heterogeneity of Treatment Effect(HTE), which has high end relevance in the research agenda of precision medicine and comparative effectiveness research [@kent_predictive_2020].
HTE refers to the non-random variation in the magnitude or direction of a treatment effect across levels of a patient attribute, or covariates against a specific clinical outcome[@varadhan_estimation_2013]. Though the ultimate aim of traditional evidence based medicine is establishing causality on a population level, the emergence of precision medicine and patient centered research has elicited interest in identifying these individual variations[@selby_predictive_2025]. HTE is classified as quantitative, when the treatment is beneficial for everyone but to different degreers, or qualitative when a treatment is beneficial for some but harmful for others[@wang_statistics_2007]. 

In spite of these developed predictive frameworks, most of clinical trial reports continue to rely on conventional subgroup analysis.[@kent_predictive_2020] This is done by dividing the trial population based on one variable at a time characteristics, such as age or sex, and try to evaluate the treatment effect variation, for instance between male and female or young versus old. Nevertheless, this traditional approach fail as it can not inform a clinician how to treat a patient who is simultaneously elderly, female, and has a low ejection fraction and a family history of myocardial infarction. A patient's response to therapy is determined by case mix clinically prognostic risk factors acting jointly, rather than isolated attributes[@bellavia_heterogeneity_2024][@califf_selection_1997]. Subgroup analysis fails to capture these multivariate treatment response patterns, by underrepresenting the heterogeneity that clinicians observe at the person level[@kent_personalized_2018]. For a patient brings not only it's sex or age while approaching a clinical setting. 

One of the reason for the low credibility of conventional subgroup is the problem of multiplicity. Unlike the primary trial analysis, which is protected by a pre-specified protocols and power calculations, subgroup analyses are frequently performed licentiously across number of baseline variables. This creates a high risk of false positive(type I error) result that increases significantly with every additional comparison conducted. [@wang_statistics_2007] By examining many variables without a clear prior hypothesis, we inevitably begin to see patterns where there are none, essentially mistaking the noise of a specific dataset for a genuine biological signal[@kent_personalized_2018][@senn_heterogeneous_2026]. For instance, if the null hypothesis is true for 10 independent test for interaction at the 0.05 significance level, the chance of at least one false positive result exceeds 40%[@wang_statistics_2007]. Such exploratory analyses usually end up in testimation bias, which is also knows as winner's curse. The reason for this bias is that researchers preferentially report exclusively those subgroups that reach a specific threshold of statistical significance, which is a p-value less than 0.05. Owing to this, observed effect sizes become inherently inflated, reflecting the most extreme and overestimated deviation from the truth.[@kent_personalized_2018]

The other reason for unreliability in subgroup analysis a significant mismatch in statistical power. RCTs are designed and powered to detect a main treatment effect in a large population, and they are hardly designed to detect interactions between subgroups. [@willke_concepts_2012] In fact, such detection may requires four fold sample size from the main treatment effect analysis. For instance, in a trial where power is 80% for the average effect, a test for a perfectly balanced subgroup(e.g young versus old) is anticipated to have power of only about 30%.[@kent_personalized_2018]
This power mismatch mostly yields false negative(Type II error) results, where treatment looks like it has consistent effect across all subgroups in forest plot, but practically the study lacked the statistical strength to detect the genuine variations[@bellavia_heterogeneity_2024]. A good example can be seen in the GUSTO-I trial. Even in a study of this great scale, there is limited statistical power to detect a quantitative interaction between a specific risk factor and the relative benefit of accelerated TPA, primarily due to low event rates. For instance, a formal test conducted to determine if the relative benefit of treatment relies on age yielded a TPA by Age interaction that has p-value of 0.23 [califf_selection_1997].In this study the estimates of the two age slopes were 0.008 and 0.0086. Mathematically, the slopes' difference would have been needed to be 0.014 instead of 0.0006 to provide 0.8 power to detect a significant differential effect of TPA according to age. This can serve as an evidence that for the purpose of external validity no trial would likely enroll sufficient elderly patients to conduct such a test with high degree of confidence, leaving hidden potential heterogeneity behind the trial average.[califf_selection_1997]

A common methodological error in conventional reporting is claiming heterogeneity based on separate tests of significance within subgroups, for example, a drug worked for women with a p-value of 0.02 but not for men with a p-value of 0.14[@wang_statistics_2007]. Statistically speaking this is not a proof of treatment effect difference between the two sexes, it only shows that the specific study duffers with lack of power to reach the significance in the smaller male group[@wang_statistics_2007]. Present guidance now requires HTE must be assessed using interaction terms in regression models which test if the difference between groups is significant, rather than testing each group in isolation[@kent_assessing_2010]. Nevertheless, testing interaction demands four times of the sample size for the main effect analysis, majority of trials remain blind to genuine variations in treatment response [@wang_statistics_2007] [@varadhan_estimation_2013].  

In contemporary medical researches, pre-planned subgroup analysis remains as a standard tool for exploring HTE.Notwithstanding, there is a growing methodological consensus that such an approach may not represent the most appropriate means of investigating individual treatment variation. [@willke_concepts_2012] This inadequacy is accentuated by a caution from the Consolidated Standard of Reporting Trials(CONSORT) statement[@gabler_dealing_2009]. In spite of these caution, univariate cuts remain dominating clinical reporting, often leading to over interpretation of chance findings[@kent_personalized_2018].

A critical conceptual error in conventional subgroup reporting is credence on the relative scale(e.g odds ratios or hazard ratios) to conclude the consistency of treatment effect[@sun_is_2010]. While relative effect often remain constant across subgroups, the absolute risk reduction(ARR) varies based on a patient's baseline risk. This mathematical relationship is known as risk magnification; as a patient's baseline risk increases, the absolute benefit he or she derive from an effective treatment also increases [@selby_predictive_2025]. Traditional subgroup analysis, focusing solely on relative scales obscures greater differences in the number of lives saved, failing to identify that a drug might be life saving for a high risk group while offering negligible benefit to a low-risk group [@kent_personalized_2018].

Beyond inability to demonstrate benefit, conventional subgroup analysis often omit net treatment harm[@kent_predictive_2020]. Almost all medical interventions does not come without a risk of some serious adverse effect, such as intracranial haemorrhage or major bleeding or other respective complications, following it's treatment benefit. For those who fall in the high baseline risk patient strata, the absolute disease preventing benefit from a drug far outweighs these complications. On the other hand, for low risk patients, the same adverse effects can totally wear down the marginal benefit [@kent_assessing_2010]. This lead to qualitative interactions where treatment cause more harm than benefit[@wang_statistics_2007][@gabler_dealing_2009]. Because patients fall into broad categories in the eyes of one variable at a time approach, where these groups usually appear treatment favorable on average by hiding the significant portion of patients who are incarcerated in a harm zone.

A major structural flaw in depending on trial average and conventional subgroups is the skewed distribution of baseline risk, referred to us the Lake Wobegon Effect. In most clinical trials, often nearly 75% of participants lies below average risk. Then the trial average effect size inevitably driven by small influential quarter of high risk outliers[@kent_personalized_2018]. Hence, adopting the trial average to a reala patient sitting in clinical setting will undoubtedly misleading and leads to systematic overtreatment of low risk individuals [greenfield_heterogeneity_2007].



In 2020, an expert panel funded by the Patient Centered Outcome Research(PCOR) published the Predictive Approaches to Treatment Effect Heterogeneity(PATH) statement[@selby_predictive_2025]. The statement was delivered from the conceived argument of that traditional RCTs fail to answer "what is the most likely outcome when this particular drug is given to a particular patient?" a question one practicing physician may raise as the epidemiologist Austin Bradford Hill argued[@kent_personalized_2018]. As a remedy, PATH framework provides guidance in conducting predictive HTE analyses by incorporating multiple clinically prognostic attributes simultaneously rather than serially dividing populations into secluded subgroups[@selby_predictive_2025].

A guiding doctrine of the PATH framework is that HTE is a scale dependent concept; its presence or absence depends on whether the effect is measured on a relative scale or an absolute scale[@kent_predictive_2020]. The PATH statement emphasizes that that HTE need to be measured both in the relative scale(e.g odds ratio) and the absolute scale(e.g risk difference), noting that the latter is far more relevant in clinical setup to making treatment decisions and also to individual patients. This shift in methodology is considered indispensably formative leap towards realizing the full potential of personalized evidence based medicine. The PATH framework gives two different approaches for predictive HTE analyses; risk modelling and effect modelling. The former disaggregates patients on the basis of baseline risk strata, while the latter directly estimates individual effects using interaction terms or machine learning algorithms. [@kent_predictive_2020] 

Risk modelling is the first line intervention that the framework recommend when RCTs yield an overall treatment effect[@kent_predictive_2020]. It is a tow step process. First, a multivariable model which is blinded to a treatment assignment used to predict each patient's baseline risk across the population for the primary outcome. Secondly, all patients will be stratified into equal sized risk quarters, to evaluate how treatment effect vary as function of different risk levels both in relative and absolute measurement scale [@selby_predictive_2025] [@kent_predictive_2020].
In contrast, effect modelling allows direct estimation of individualized treatment effects[@kent_personalized_2018]. This will be computed using regression models that incorporate multiplicative interaction terms or modern, non-parametric machine learning algorithms such as random forests or causal forests[@selby_predictive_2025]. Since these models look for interactions, they are highly vulnerable to overfitting and testimation bias[@kent_predictive_2020]. Recently conducted scoping review from 65 reports that implemented the PATH statment highlighted a crucial insights to the credibility of predictive methods. It states that risk based modeling was significantly with 87% credibility rate, more likely to yield credible and reproducible findings than effect modeling. Owing to this, the PATH framework suggests effect modelling findings to be externally validated in independent datasets to establish their clinical credibility[@selby_predictive_2025]. 


The primary objective of this research is to implement and evaluate the PATH(Predictive Approaches to Treatment effect Heterogeneity) framework across four large clinical trial datasets; Digitalis Investigation Group Trial, International Stroke Trial, the GUSTO-I trial, and The Vitamin D and Omega-3 Trial, to determine its utility in providing patient centered evidence than traditional population average and one variable at a time approach in traditional subgroup analysis. This paper will implement predictive HTE analysis to compare patient centered estimates of outcome risks under intervention versus under control, while accounting clinically prognostic patient attributes simultaneously. This investigation will apply suitable statistical and machine learning methods to predict patient outcomes, including logistic regression, cox proportional hazard models and random forest respectively. Considering the PATH statement guidelines, the paper aims to apply this predictive risk models to estimate the benefit of experimental treatments under different levels of baseline risk.

A secondary aim is to employ Monte Carlo simulations designed under the Aim Data-generating mechanism Estimand, Method and Performance(ADEMP) structure to evaluate the Type I error behavior of risk based interaction tests,ensuring that identified heterogeneity represents a reproducible clinical signal rather than statistical noise. Ultimately, this paper try to show the treatment benefit predictions and their associated uncertainty to bridge the gap between group level trail results and the particular patient sitting in the clinical cockpit. 

The remainder of this report is structured to evaluate the predictive approaches and their reflection for clinical care. The method section describe the statistical model specification and computational implementation for each of the four trials. It will also bring to visibility the novel statistical method of ADEMP simulation framework. The results section presents findings through PATH compatible forest plots and Absolute benefit curves, empirically demonstrating the mathematical reality of risk magnification.

In the end, the discussion synthesizes these results to map the policy and reporting implications for clinical guidelines, trying to address the structural barriers to transitioning from population averages toward a more patient centered evidence based medicine.


# Limitation and Future work

Some critical constraints must be considered when interpreting findings from this projects. Data related limitations are the primary concern. In the DIG trial we used the teaching dataset,in which most variables were permuted over the set of patients within treatment groups to make sure complete anonymisation [@chern_biochemical_1976]. This permutation process means that multidimensional relationships not explicitly documented in the original report may not have been preserved. As a result the validity of multivariate inferences derived from this specific teaching dataset potentially compromised[@chern_biochemical_1976]. Furthermore, while the National Lung Screening Trial(NLST) was initially targeted to evaluate the PATH framework to the domain of cancer screening, the unavailability of NLST data neccessiated a transition to the VITAL trial dataset for the final empirical analysis.

Beyond these, this project is subject to the inherent lack of statistical power for interaction test in conventional RCTs, which are primarily designed to detect average treatment effects rather than heterogeneity[@senn_heterogeneous_2026]. There may be limited power to detect genuine variation in large trials including GUSTO-I which leads to a risk of false negatives(Type I errors)[@califf_selection_1997]. 

In addition, since patients in these parallel arm trials only receive one intervention, individual treatment effect are technically unobservable, as a result the models provide conditional average treatment effects for reference classes rather than direct measures of a unique individual's response[@kent_predictive_2020][@kent_personalized_2018]. 

Future work may go beyond primary outcome risk by integrating treatment related harms into predictive models, to allow benefit harm trade off analysis across different risk strata[[@kent_predictive_2020][@kent_personalized_2018]. To amplify the clinical credibility of these findings, the identified models should undergo external validation and calibration in independent patient cohorts to make sure applicability to real world population [@selby_predictive_2025][@kent_predictive_2020]. Methodologically, in future research works we plan to implement decision curve analysis as a valuable step to evaluate whether a "treat only those above a specific risk threshold" strategy is superior than to treat everyone[@selby_predictive_2025][@kent_predictive_2020]. Finally, further investigation is still indispensable to determine if tree based machine learning algorithms including causal forests provide distinct predictive advantages over traditional regression based approaches for determining patient specific benefit in these clinical contexts[@kent_predictive_2020][@kent_personalized_2018].
